mainEntity.name: What is a class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A class in Java is a blueprint or template for creating objects. It defines the state (fields/variables) and behaviour (methods) that all objects of that type will share. A class is declared using the 'class' keyword. Everything in Java exists inside a class — there are no standalone variables or functions. When you create an object using 'new ClassName()', Java allocates memory based on the class blueprint and returns a reference to that object.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A class is the BLUEPRINT — it defines what fields and methods objects of that type will have. No memory is allocated for data when a class is declared. An object is an INSTANCE — a concrete entity in memory created from the class blueprint using 'new'. Each object has its own copy of instance fields. Analogy: a class is like the architectural drawing of a house; an object is the actual house built from that drawing. You can build many houses (objects) from one drawing (class).

mainEntity.name: What is a constructor in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A constructor is a special method that is automatically called when an object is created using 'new'. It initialises the object's state. Rules: the constructor name MUST match the class name exactly, it has NO return type (not even void), and it can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different parameter lists). If you write no constructor, Java provides a default no-argument constructor automatically. If you write any constructor, the default one is NOT provided.

mainEntity.name: What is the 'this' keyword in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 'this' keyword in Java is a reference to the CURRENT object — the instance on which the method or constructor is being called. It is used to: (1) Distinguish instance variables from parameters with the same name: 'this.name = name'. (2) Call another constructor in the same class: 'this(args)' — constructor chaining. (3) Pass the current object as an argument to another method. (4) Return the current object from a method (builder/fluent pattern). 'this' is only available in instance context — not in static methods.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between instance methods and static methods in a class?

acceptedAnswer.text: Instance methods belong to an OBJECT — they require an object to be called (object.method()), can access both instance and static fields, and can use 'this'. Static methods belong to the CLASS — called without an object (ClassName.method()), can only access static fields directly, and cannot use 'this'. Use instance methods for behaviour that depends on object state. Use static methods for utility operations that don't need object state (e.g., Math.sqrt(), Integer.parseInt()).

sections.title: What is a Class in Java?

blocks.text: A class in Java is the most fundamental building block of object-oriented programming. It is a blueprint or template that defines: (1) the state an object holds — represented by fields (variables), and (2) the behaviour an object can perform — represented by methods. A class itself occupies no memory for data — it is only when you create an object from the class that memory is allocated.

In Java, everything lives inside a class. There are no standalone variables or functions at the top level of a file. Every field, every method, every constructor must be declared inside a class body. This is what makes Java a purely object-oriented language at the structural level — the class is the mandatory container for all code.

Real-world analogy: think of a class as an architectural blueprint for a house. The blueprint defines how many rooms there are (fields), what each room is for, and what actions can be performed in the house (methods). Using the blueprint, you can construct many actual houses (objects) — each one is a separate physical structure with its own rooms, but all follow the same blueprint design.

blocks.title: 🔑 A Java Class at a Glance
blocks.text: A class typically contains: (1) Fields — state variables (instance or static). (2) Constructors — special methods for initialising new objects. (3) Instance methods — operations on object state. (4) Static methods — class-level utility operations. (5) Getters & Setters — controlled access to private fields. (6) Optionally: inner classes, constants, initialiser blocks. The class keyword, an access modifier, and a name are the minimum to declare a valid class.

sections.title: Class Declaration & Syntax — Anatomy of a Java Class

blocks.text: A Java class declaration follows a specific structure. Understanding each part is essential before writing any class.

items.title: Full Syntax
Class Naming Rules
items.text:
• Must start with a letter, $ or _ (not a digit)
• PascalCase convention: every word capitalised — BankAccount, OrderService, HttpRequest
• Should be a NOUN or noun phrase — represents a thing, not an action
• Match the filename exactly (case-sensitive) for public classes
• Avoid: Manager, Helper, Utils as standalone names — too vague

items.title: Class Modifiers
items.text:
Access modifiers: public (any package), default/package-private (same package only).
Non-access modifiers:
• final — class cannot be subclassed (e.g., String, Integer)
• abstract — class cannot be instantiated; may have abstract methods
• strictfp — floating-point calculations use strict IEEE 754
Top-level classes cannot be private or protected.

blocks.text: The distinction between a class and an object is the cornerstone of object-oriented programming. Confusing the two leads to some of the most common Java mistakes — especially the infamous 'non-static field cannot be referenced from a static context' compile error.

lines: // Fields defined in CLASS — each OBJECT gets its own copy
public Student(String name, int rollNumber, double cgpa) {
// ✅ Creating OBJECTS from the Student CLASS
// Each object has its OWN separate copy of fields
s1.introduce(); // Hi, I am Ravi (Roll: 101), CGPA: 8.5
s2.introduce(); // Hi, I am Priya (Roll: 102), CGPA: 9.2
s3.introduce(); // Hi, I am Arjun (Roll: 103), CGPA: 7.8
// Modifying one object does NOT affect others
// null reference — variable declared but no object created
// s4.introduce(); // ❌ NullPointerException — no object behind s4

blocks.title: ⚠️ Reference vs Object — Critical Distinction
blocks.text: 'Student s1 = new Student("Ravi", 101, 8.5);' creates TWO things: (1) The reference variable 's1' on the stack — holds the memory address. (2) The Student object on the heap — holds the actual field values. 's1' does NOT contain the object — it contains the ADDRESS where the object lives. This is why assigning 's2 = s1' does NOT copy the object — both s1 and s2 now point to the SAME object. Modifying through s2 affects what s1 sees — they share one object.

Fields (also called member variables or class variables) represent the state of a class. Every object gets its own copy of instance fields, while static fields are shared across all objects of the class. Field design is one of the most important decisions in class design — the wrong choice here leads to fragile, unmaintainable objects.

items.title: Instance Fields
items.text: Declared without 'static'. Each object gets its own separate copy. Hold the unique state for that particular object. Example: in a Student class, 'String name' and 'double cgpa' are instance fields — every student has their own name and cgpa. Accessed through an object reference: student.name. Best practice: always private — expose through getter/setter.

items.title: Static Fields
items.text: Declared with 'static'. Only ONE copy exists per class — shared by ALL objects. Changes to a static field through any object are visible to all other objects. Used for: counters (totalStudents), constants (MAX_RETRIES), shared configuration. Accessed via class name: Student.totalStudents. Best practice: static mutable fields are risky in multi-threaded programs — prefer static final constants.

items.title: final Fields
items.text: 'final' means the field can only be assigned ONCE — either at declaration or in the constructor. For primitives: the value is immutable. For objects: the reference cannot be reassigned (but the object's internal state can still be mutated). 'private final String id;' set in constructor = effectively immutable ID. Static final = a constant: 'public static final double PI = 3.14159;'. Immutable fields make objects thread-safe and easier to reason about.

items.title: Field Initialisation Order
items.text: Fields are initialised in this order: (1) Static fields and static initialiser blocks (when the class is first loaded — once only). (2) Instance fields set to their default values (0, false, null). (3) Instance field declarations with initialiser expressions. (4) Constructor body executes. This order matters when one field's default value depends on another — always initialise in constructor for clarity.

blocks.text: A constructor is a special block of code that is automatically called when an object is created using the new keyword. Its sole purpose is to initialise the object's state — setting field values, validating inputs, and setting up any initial conditions. A properly written constructor guarantees that an object is always in a valid, consistent state from the moment of creation.

items.title: Constructor Rules
items.text:
1. Name MUST exactly match the class name (case-sensitive)
2. NO return type — not even void
3. Can have any access modifier (public, private, protected, default)
4. Can be overloaded (multiple constructors with different params)
5. If no constructor is written, Java provides a default no-arg constructor
6. If ANY constructor is written, the default is NOT provided automatically

items.title: Constructor Chaining — this()
items.text: 'this(args)' inside a constructor calls ANOTHER constructor in the same class. Must be the FIRST statement in the constructor. Used to avoid code duplication when multiple constructors share setup logic. Example: a no-arg constructor can call a full constructor with default values: 'this("Unknown", 0)'. This is the DRY principle applied to constructors.

items.title: super() — Parent Constructor
items.text: 'super(args)' calls the PARENT class constructor. Must be the FIRST statement in a subclass constructor. If not explicitly written, Java automatically inserts 'super()' (no-arg parent constructor). If the parent has no no-arg constructor, the subclass MUST explicitly call super(args) — otherwise compile error. Used in inheritance to initialise the parent portion of the object.

items.title: private Constructor — Control Creation
items.text: A private constructor prevents external instantiation. Used in: (1) Singleton pattern — only one instance ever exists. (2) Utility class — all static methods, no instantiation needed. (3) Factory method pattern — object creation controlled through a static factory method that validates inputs before constructing. Example: 'LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 20)' is a factory method that validates the date before constructing.

blocks.title: 💡 Default Constructor Rule — Most Asked Trap
blocks.text: If you write NO constructor, Java provides a default no-arg constructor automatically. The moment you write ANY constructor (even a full one), Java STOPS providing the default. This catches many beginners: they write 'public MyClass(String name)' and then try 'new MyClass()' — compile error because the no-arg constructor no longer exists. Fix: either add an explicit no-arg constructor, or always use the constructors you defined.

sections.title: Instance Methods in a Class — Behaviour of Objects

blocks.text: An instance method defines the behaviour of an object. It operates on the object's own state (instance fields) and can read or modify them. Instance methods represent the verbs of a class — what objects of that type can do. Every instance method implicitly receives a this reference — a pointer to the current object — allowing it to access the calling object's fields and other methods.

items.title: Command Methods (Mutators)
items.text: Instance methods that CHANGE the object's state. Examples: deposit(double amount), withdraw(double amount), addItem(Item item), deactivate(). They typically return void or a status value (boolean for success/failure). Should validate inputs before modifying state. Never expose raw field mutation — always wrap it in a method with business rules.

items.title: Query Methods (Accessors)
items.text: Instance methods that READ and return information about the object's state without modifying it. Examples: getBalance(), isActive(), calculateTax(), toString(). Should have NO side effects — calling a query method multiple times should give the same result. Boolean queries should be named with 'is', 'has', or 'can': isAvailable(), hasPermission(), canWithdraw(amount).

items.title: Collaboration Methods
items.text: Instance methods that coordinate between objects — one object calls methods on another. Example: orderService.placeOrder(cart, payment) — the OrderService object collaborates with Cart and Payment objects. These methods are the 'glue' of object-oriented systems. They should delegate to other objects' methods rather than reaching into their internals (Law of Demeter).

sections.title: Static Fields & Static Methods — Class-Level Members

blocks.text: The static keyword on a field or method makes it belong to the class itself rather than to any individual object. Static members exist independently of any instance — they are created when the class is loaded and exist for the lifetime of the application. Understanding when to use static — and when NOT to — is a key design skill.

items.title: Static Fields — Shared State
items.text: One copy shared by ALL objects. Changes through any object are visible to all. Common uses: object counters (totalCreated++), shared configuration, caches, constants (static final). Risk: static mutable fields cause subtle bugs in multi-threaded environments and make testing harder (state persists between tests). Prefer static FINAL (constants) over mutable static fields.

items.title: Static Methods — Class-Level Operations
items.text: No 'this' reference — no access to instance fields. Used for: pure utility functions (Math.sqrt), factory methods (LocalDate.of), helper operations that don't need object state. Cannot be overridden in subclasses (method hiding, not overriding). Can be called without creating an object — ClassName.method().

items.title: Static Initialiser Block
items.text: A 'static { ... }' block runs ONCE when the class is first loaded by the JVM — before any constructor or static method call. Used for: complex static field initialisation, loading configuration files, setting up static caches. Multiple static blocks run in the order they appear in the class. Cannot throw checked exceptions.

sections.title: The 'this' Keyword — Referring to the Current Object

blocks.text: The this keyword in Java is a reference to the current object — the specific instance on which the method or constructor is currently executing. It is one of the most frequently used and most misunderstood keywords in Java, essential for writing clear class code.

items.title: Use 1 — Resolve Name Conflicts (Most Common)
items.text: 'this.name = name;' — when a constructor or setter parameter has the same name as the instance field, 'this.fieldName' refers to the field and 'paramName' (without this) refers to the parameter. Without 'this', both refer to the parameter — the field is never set. This is the most common use of 'this' in Java code.

items.title: Use 2 — Constructor Chaining (this())
items.text: 'this(args)' inside a constructor calls another constructor in the SAME class. Must be the VERY FIRST statement in the constructor — before any other code. Used to avoid duplicating initialisation logic across multiple constructors. The chain of constructors ultimately leads to the one that does all the real initialisation work.

items.title: Use 3 — Pass Current Object as Argument
items.text: 'someMethod(this)' passes the current object as an argument to another method. Common in event handling: 'button.addListener(this)'. Also used in builder and fluent interface patterns: 'return this;' at the end of a setter returns the current object, enabling method chaining: 'builder.setName("X").setAge(25).build()'.

items.title: 'this' Cannot Be Used in static Context
items.text: Static methods belong to the class, not to any object — there is NO current object. Therefore 'this' cannot be used inside a static method or static initialiser block. Attempting to do so is a compile error: 'non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context'. This is the same reason you cannot access instance fields from a static method.

blocks.label: ThisKeywordDemo.java
lines: // ── Use 1: Resolve field vs parameter name conflict ──
public Person(String name, int age, String city) {
// ── Use 3: Return 'this' for method chaining (Fluent API) ──
return this; // Returns current object for chaining
if (age < 0 || age > 150) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid age");
// ── Use 3b: Pass 'this' as argument to another method ──
// Person p2 = new Person("Priya"); // name=Priya, age=0, city=Unknown
// Person p3 = new Person("Arjun", 25); // name=Arjun, age=25, city=Unknown

sections.title: Getter & Setter Methods — Controlled Field Access

blocks.text: Getter and setter methods are the standard mechanism for providing controlled external access to private fields. They are the practical implementation of encapsulation: keep fields private, expose them through methods that can enforce validation, add logging, trigger events, or compute derived values.

items.title: Getter — Read Access
items.text: Returns the value of a private field. Naming: 'get' + FieldName in PascalCase for most types: getName(), getBalance(), getCategory(). Boolean fields: 'is' + FieldName: isActive(), isVerified(), isPremium(). Getters should be simple and NEVER have side effects — they should only read and return, never modify state.

items.title: Setter — Write Access with Validation
items.text: Sets a private field value — the KEY advantage over public fields is built-in validation. Naming: 'set' + FieldName: setName(), setBalance(). Should validate before assigning: null checks, range checks, format checks. Can throw exceptions for invalid input. Can trigger side effects: update a timestamp, fire a change event, recalculate a derived value.

items.title: Read-Only Fields — Getter Without Setter
items.text: Some fields should be immutable after construction — provide a getter but NO setter. Example: userId set in constructor should never change. Making a field final + getter-only enforces immutability at the language level. This is safer than just 'forgetting' to write a setter — final prevents accidental reassignment even inside the class.

items.title: Computed Properties — Getter Without Stored Field
items.text: Not every getter needs a corresponding stored field. Some values can be COMPUTED on demand: 'getFullName() { return firstName + " " + lastName; }'. Or 'getAge() { return Period.between(birthDate, LocalDate.now()).getYears(); }'. Computed getters eliminate synchronisation issues — there is no stored age to become stale. Calculate from source data, not from a cached copy.

sections.title: Inner Classes (Nested Classes) — Classes Inside Classes

blocks.text: Java allows declaring a class inside another class. These are called nested classes or inner classes. They are used to logically group classes that are only used in one place, increase encapsulation, and produce more readable and maintainable code. Java has four types of nested classes, each with distinct characteristics.

items.title: Non-static Inner Class
items.text: Declared inside a class without 'static'. Has access to ALL members of the outer class — including private fields. Requires an outer class object to be created: 'Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner()'. Use for: iterator implementations, event listeners tightly coupled to their outer class. Avoid if the inner class doesn't truly need access to the outer class instance.

items.title: Static Nested Class
items.text: Declared inside a class WITH 'static'. Does NOT have access to instance members of the outer class — only static members. Created without an outer class object: 'Outer.StaticNested obj = new Outer.StaticNested()'. Preferred over non-static inner class when the nested class doesn't need outer instance access. Used for: builder classes (Person.Builder), grouped helper classes, namespace organisation.

items.title: Local Class
items.text: Declared INSIDE a method body. Visible only within that method. Can access local variables of the enclosing method if they are effectively final. Rarely used in modern Java — lambdas and anonymous classes typically serve the same purpose more concisely.

items.title: Anonymous Class
items.text: A class with no name — declared and instantiated in the same expression. Commonly used to implement interfaces or extend abstract classes with a one-off implementation: 'Runnable r = new Runnable() { public void run() { ... } };'. In modern Java (8+), lambdas replace anonymous classes for functional interfaces. Still used for abstract classes and multi-method interfaces.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Trip Everyone Up

blocks.text: These class-and-method mistakes are consistently found in Java beginner and intermediate code. Each one either causes a compile-time error or a subtle runtime bug that is hard to diagnose.

blocks.label: ClassMethodMistakes.java
lines: name = name; // ❌ Assigns parameter to itself! Field 'this.name' stays null
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Accessing instance member from static context
System.out.println(count); // ❌ Compile error — no 'this' in static
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Calling this() NOT as first statement
this(width, height, "blue"); // ❌ Compile error — must be FIRST
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Writing return type on constructor
// void Circle(double radius) { } // ❌ This is a METHOD named 'Circle', not a constructor
// It will never be called by 'new Circle(...)' — silent logical error
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: Default constructor disappears after writing one
// Config c = new Config(); // ❌ Compile error — no-arg constructor gone
// ✅ Fix: explicitly add no-arg constructor if still needed
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Returning mutable internal collection from getter
return members; // ❌ Caller gets direct reference — can modify!
// ❌ MISTAKE 7: NullPointerException from uninitialized object field
private List<String> items; // ❌ Null — not initialised

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These class design anti-patterns are the most common causes of failed code reviews in professional Java teams. Each violates fundamental OOP principles and creates long-term maintenance nightmares.

items.title: God Class — Does Everything
items.text: A single class with 50+ fields, 100+ methods, handling every concern of the application. Violates Single Responsibility Principle. Signs: class name ends in Manager, Service, Handler, Processor doing unrelated things. Fix: split by responsibility — UserRegistrationService, UserAuthenticationService, UserProfileService. Each class should have ONE reason to change.

items.title: Anemic Domain Model
items.text: A class that is just a data bag — only private fields and public getters/setters, no business logic. The business logic is scattered across 'service' classes that directly manipulate the domain object's state. Fix: move behaviour INTO the domain class. An 'Account' class should have deposit(), withdraw(), calculateInterest() — not just getBalance()/setBalance().

items.title: Mutable Object Without Thread Safety
items.text: A class with mutable state accessed by multiple threads without synchronisation. 'counter++' is NOT atomic — it is read-modify-write in three steps. Two threads can both read 5, both increment to 6, and both write 6 — losing one increment. Fix: use immutable objects where possible, AtomicInteger for counters, or synchronised/volatile for shared mutable state.

items.title: Long Parameter List in Constructor
items.text: A constructor with 7+ parameters is a code smell. Hard to call correctly, easy to swap adjacent arguments of the same type (price and stock both int — very easy to mix up). Fix: use the Builder pattern for classes with many optional parameters. Or group related parameters into dedicated value objects: 'Address address' instead of 'String street, String city, String state, String pincode'.

items.title: No equals()/hashCode() on Value Objects
items.text: Using objects as Map keys or Set elements without overriding equals() and hashCode() means Java uses REFERENCE equality (identity) — two 'equal' objects are treated as different. Example: two ProductId objects with the same id String will not be found as equal without overriding these methods. Rule: whenever you override equals(), you MUST override hashCode() with the same fields — contracts require this.

items.title: Calling Overridable Methods in Constructor
items.text: Calling a non-final, non-private (i.e., overridable) method inside a constructor is dangerous in an inheritance hierarchy. If a subclass overrides that method and the subclass's constructor hasn't run yet, the overridden version runs before the subclass fields are initialised — accessing uninitialised fields. Fix: only call private or final methods from constructors.

blocks.label: ClassAntiPatterns.java
lines: // ❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Calling overridable method in constructor
initialise(); // ❌ Dangerous if overridden in subclass
super(); // Base() calls initialise() before Derived() sets config
// ❌ config is null here! Derived() hasn't run yet
// ✅ Fix: make initialise() private or final in Base
// ❌ ANTI-PATTERN: No equals/hashCode — broken Set/Map behaviour
// set.contains(new ProductId("P001")); // ❌ Returns false! Different object
// ✅ Fix: override both equals and hashCode
if (!(o instanceof ProductId p)) return false;

sections.title: Java Class & Methods Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced developer interviews, campus placements, and OCPJP/OCA certification exams.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
items.a: A class is the BLUEPRINT — a template that defines what fields (state) and methods (behaviour) objects of that type will have. Declaring a class allocates NO memory for field data — it is only metadata. An object is an INSTANCE — a concrete entity in memory created from the class using 'new'. Each object has its own copy of instance fields on the Java Heap. One class → many objects. Analogy: a class is the cookie-cutter mould; objects are the actual cookies cut from it. Key JVM distinction: class metadata is stored in the Method Area (Metaspace); object data is stored on the Heap.

items.q: Q2. What are the rules for writing a constructor in Java?
items.a: A Java constructor must follow these rules: (1) Name must exactly match the class name — case-sensitive. (2) No return type — not even void. Writing a return type makes it a regular method, not a constructor. (3) Can have any access modifier: public, private, protected, or default. (4) Can be overloaded — multiple constructors with different parameter lists. (5) Can call another constructor in the same class using 'this(args)' — must be the first statement. (6) Can call the parent constructor using 'super(args)' — also must be the first statement (cannot have both this() and super()). (7) If NO constructor is written, Java provides a default no-arg constructor automatically. Once ANY constructor is written, the default is NOT provided.

items.q: Q3. What is the purpose of the 'this' keyword in Java?
items.a: The 'this' keyword refers to the CURRENT OBJECT — the instance on which the method/constructor is executing. Four main uses: (1) Resolve naming conflict between instance field and local parameter: 'this.name = name'. (2) Constructor chaining within the same class: 'this(args)' — must be first statement. (3) Pass the current object as an argument: 'register(this)'. (4) Return the current object for method chaining / fluent API: 'return this'. Important: 'this' is ONLY available in instance context — it is NOT available in static methods or static initialiser blocks, because static members have no associated object.

items.q: Q4. What happens if you don't define any constructor in a Java class?
items.a: Java automatically provides a DEFAULT no-argument constructor with public access. This default constructor calls 'super()' (the parent's no-arg constructor) implicitly. It initialises all fields to their default values: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for objects. IMPORTANT: the moment you write ANY explicit constructor — even one with parameters — Java STOPS providing the default constructor. This is the source of a very common compile error: developers add a parameterised constructor, then try 'new MyClass()' and get a 'no suitable constructor found' error.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between instance variables and static variables?
items.a: Instance variables: declared without 'static'. Each object gets its OWN separate copy — stored on the Heap as part of the object. Changes to one object's instance variable don't affect other objects. Exist as long as the object exists. Static variables: declared with 'static'. ONE copy per class — shared by ALL instances. Stored in the Method Area (Metaspace). Changes through any reference affect all references. Exist for the lifetime of the application. Example: 'String name' (instance — every Employee has their own name). 'int employeeCount' with static (shared — all Employees share one counter). Access: instance var through object reference; static var through class name (preferred) or object reference.

items.q: Q6. Can we call an instance method from a static method in Java?
items.a: Not directly — you first need an object. A static method belongs to the class and has no 'this' reference. So calling an instance method directly (without an object) is a compile error: 'non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context'. Fix: create an object first. Example inside main(): 'MyClass obj = new MyClass(); obj.instanceMethod();'. Exception: if you receive an object as a parameter: 'public static void process(MyClass obj) { obj.instanceMethod(); }' — this is valid because the object reference is explicit. This is a fundamental consequence of the class/instance distinction.

items.q: Q7. What is constructor chaining in Java? How does this() differ from super()?
items.a: 'this(args)' calls another constructor in the SAME class — used to avoid duplicating initialisation code across overloaded constructors. 'super(args)' calls a constructor in the PARENT class — used to initialise the parent portion of the object. Both must be the VERY FIRST statement in the constructor — so they cannot both appear together (having both 'this()' and 'super()' in the same constructor is a compile error). 'this()' eventually leads to one constructor that calls 'super()'. If neither is written, Java auto-inserts 'super()'. If the parent has no no-arg constructor, the subclass MUST explicitly call 'super(args)' — compile error otherwise.

items.q: Q8. What is the static initialiser block? When does it run?
items.a: A static initialiser block is written as 'static { ... }' inside a class. It runs EXACTLY ONCE when the class is first loaded by the JVM — before any constructor or static method call, and before any object is created. Used for: complex static field initialisation (loading config files, building lookup maps, setting up caches). Multiple static blocks run in the order they appear. They cannot throw checked exceptions (wrap in try-catch or use a static method). Contrast with the instance initialiser block '{ ... }' (no static keyword) — that runs each time an object is created, before the constructor body, after field initialisers.

items.q: Q9. Why should we always override hashCode() when we override equals()?
items.a: The Java contract requires: objects that are equal (equals() returns true) MUST have the same hashCode(). If you override equals() without overriding hashCode(), you violate this contract. Consequence: HashMap, HashSet, Hashtable use hashCode() first to find the bucket, then equals() to confirm. If two 'equal' objects have different hashCodes, they land in different buckets — HashMap.get() or Set.contains() will fail to find the object even though equals() would return true. Rule: whenever you override equals(), override hashCode() using the same fields. Java 7+: use Objects.hash(field1, field2) for a clean, consistent implementation.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between a static nested class and a non-static inner class?
items.a: Static nested class: declared with 'static' keyword inside another class. Does NOT have access to the outer class's instance members — only static members. Created WITHOUT an outer class object: 'Outer.StaticNested obj = new Outer.StaticNested()'. Preferred in most cases — common use: Builder pattern. Non-static inner class: declared without 'static'. Has access to ALL members of the outer class (including private instance fields) via an implicit reference to the outer instance. Requires an outer class object to exist: 'Outer outer = new Outer(); Outer.Inner inner = outer.new Inner()'. Used for: iterator implementations, event listeners tightly coupled to outer class. Key memory concern: a non-static inner class holds an implicit reference to its outer class instance — this can prevent garbage collection of the outer object.

Bug: 'radius = radius' assigns the parameter to itself — the instance field 'this.radius' is never set and stays at its default value of 0.0. So getArea() always returns 0.0, regardless of the constructor argument. Fix: 'this.radius = radius;' — 'this.radius' refers to the instance field, plain 'radius' refers to the parameter. This is the classic 'missing this' bug. Best prevention: some teams prefix fields with 'f_' or use IDE warnings for self-assignment, but the standard Java approach is consistent use of 'this.field'.

COMPILE ERROR in Car's constructor. Vehicle has only one constructor: Vehicle(String brand). Java auto-inserts 'super()' (no-arg parent constructor) as the first line of Car's constructor if no explicit super() call is written. But Vehicle has NO no-arg constructor — once you write any constructor, the default disappears. Fix: 'public Car(String brand, int doors) { super(brand); this.doors = doors; }'. Alternatively, add an explicit no-arg constructor to Vehicle: 'public Vehicle() { this("Unknown"); }'.

items.q: 4. Design a class 'Rectangle' with: length and width (private), constructor, getArea(), getPerimeter(), isSquare(), and toString(). All fields must be positive.
items.a: public class Rectangle { private final double length; private final double width; public Rectangle(double length, double width) { if (length <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Length must be positive"); if (width <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Width must be positive"); this.length = length; this.width = width; } public double getLength()      { return length; } public double getWidth()       { return width; } public double getArea()        { return length * width; } public double getPerimeter()   { return 2 * (length + width); } public boolean isSquare()      { return Double.compare(length, width) == 0; } @Override public String toString() { return String.format("Rectangle[%.2f x %.2f | Area: %.2f | Perimeter: %.2f%s]", length, width, getArea(), getPerimeter(), isSquare() ? " | Square" : ""); } } // Note: 'final' fields because a rectangle's dimensions don't change after creation. 'Double.compare' for floating-point equality — never use == with doubles.

Output: 'Parent static block', 'Child static block', 'Parent instance block', 'Parent constructor', 'Child instance block', 'Child constructor', 'Parent instance block', 'Parent constructor', 'Child instance block', 'Child constructor'. Order explanation: Static blocks run ONCE on class load — Parent is loaded first (Child extends it), then Child. For EACH 'new Child()': (1) Parent instance block, (2) Parent constructor, (3) Child instance block, (4) Child constructor. Static blocks do NOT repeat. Instance blocks and constructors repeat for each new object. The parent's instance block and constructor always run before the child's.

items.q: 6. Implement a Thread-safe Singleton class in Java.
items.a: public class AppConfig { // Volatile ensures visibility across threads private static volatile AppConfig instance; private final String environment; private AppConfig() { this.environment = System.getProperty("app.env", "production"); } // Double-checked locking pattern public static AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) { // First check — no lock synchronized (AppConfig.class) { if (instance == null) { // Second check — with lock instance = new AppConfig(); } } } return instance; } public String getEnvironment() { return environment; } } // Alternative — Bill Pugh Singleton (preferred, lazy, thread-safe, no synchronisation overhead): public class AppConfig { private AppConfig() { } private static class Holder { private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig(); } public static AppConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } // Bill Pugh uses class loading guarantees to ensure thread safety without explicit synchronization.

Three bugs: (1) No null check — 'obj == null' will cause a ClassCastException or NullPointerException. (2) No type check — 'obj' might not be a Student. Casting without instanceof will throw ClassCastException if a different type is passed. (3) Missing hashCode() — equals() is overridden but hashCode() is not, violating the equals-hashCode contract, breaking HashMap/HashSet. Fixed version: @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; if (!(o instanceof Student s)) return false; return this.id == s.id; } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id); }

items.q: 8. Implement a Builder pattern for a class 'EmailMessage' with: to (required), from (required), subject (optional), body (optional), isHtml (optional, default false), priority (optional, default NORMAL).
items.a: public final class EmailMessage { public enum Priority { LOW, NORMAL, HIGH } private final String to; private final String from; private final String subject; private final String body; private final boolean isHtml; private final Priority priority; private EmailMessage(Builder b) { this.to=b.to; this.from=b.from; this.subject=b.subject!=null?b.subject:""; this.body=b.body!=null?b.body:""; this.isHtml=b.isHtml; this.priority=b.priority; } public static class Builder { private final String to; private final String from; private String subject; private String body; private boolean isHtml=false; private Priority priority=Priority.NORMAL; public Builder(String to, String from) { if(to==null||!to.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid to"); if(from==null||!from.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid from"); this.to=to; this.from=from; } public Builder subject(String s){this.subject=s;return this;} public Builder body(String b){this.body=b;return this;} public Builder html(){this.isHtml=true;return this;} public Builder priority(Priority p){this.priority=p;return this;} public EmailMessage build(){return new EmailMessage(this);} } // Usage: EmailMessage.Builder("a@b.com","c@d.com").subject("Hi").body("Hello").priority(Priority.HIGH).build(); }

sections.title: Conclusion — Classes & Methods: The Heart of Java OOP

blocks.text: The class is the fundamental unit of object-oriented programming in Java. Every field, every constructor, every method — all live inside a class. Mastering class design is not just about knowing the syntax — it is about understanding how to model real-world entities with appropriate state, behaviour, and encapsulation.

The hallmarks of a well-designed Java class are clear: private fields with controlled access, constructors that guarantee valid state, methods that each do one thing, proper equals/hashCode for value objects, and meaningful toString for debugging. The Builder pattern for complex objects, factory methods for controlled creation, and the static nested class for grouped helpers — these patterns turn average Java code into production-grade software.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Class & Methods

items.q: What is a class in Java?
items.a: A class in Java is a blueprint or template for creating objects. It defines the state (fields) and behaviour (methods) that all objects of that type will share. Everything in Java exists inside a class — there are no standalone variables or functions. When you create an object using 'new ClassName()', Java allocates memory on the Heap based on the class blueprint. One class can produce many independent objects, each with its own copy of instance fields.

items.q: What is the difference between a class and an object in Java?
items.a: A class is the BLUEPRINT — defines structure and behaviour, allocates no field data. An object is an INSTANCE — a concrete entity in memory with its own field values, created from the class using 'new'. One class definition → unlimited objects. Class metadata lives in the Method Area; object data lives on the Heap. Analogy: the class is the architectural drawing of a house; the object is the actual house built from that drawing.

items.q: What is a constructor in Java?
items.a: A constructor is a special block that runs automatically when an object is created using 'new'. Rules: name must match the class name exactly; no return type (not even void); can be overloaded; if none is written Java provides a default no-arg constructor; if any constructor is written the default disappears. Constructors initialise object state and should validate inputs to ensure objects are always in a valid state from the moment of creation.

items.q: What is the 'this' keyword in Java?
items.a: The 'this' keyword is a reference to the current object — the instance on which the method or constructor is executing. Uses: (1) Resolve field vs parameter name conflict: 'this.name = name'. (2) Call another constructor in the same class: 'this(args)' — must be first statement. (3) Pass the current object as an argument. (4) Return the current object for method chaining: 'return this'. Not available in static methods — static context has no current object.

items.q: What is the difference between instance methods and static methods in a class?
items.a: Instance methods belong to an OBJECT — require an object to call (object.method()), have access to both instance and static members, and can use 'this'. Static methods belong to the CLASS — called without an object (ClassName.method()), can only directly access static members, and cannot use 'this'. Use instance methods for behaviour that depends on object state. Use static for utility operations that don't need object state — Math.sqrt(), Integer.parseInt(), factory methods.
